data.title: Šimunky – a hillfort on the white crags above Dolná Mariková
data.excerpt: About 1.5 km north-west of Dolná Mariková, white dolomite crags rise above the trees; the widest of them, Široká, carried a hillfort so well protected by vertical rock faces that it hardly needed fortifying. Spurs, axe-shaped currency bars, tools and a mass of nomadic arrowheads tell of a Great Moravian centre guarding an old route towards Moravia, which fell to an Old Hungarian assault at the beginning of the 10th century.
data.metaTitle: Šimunky – hillfort on the crags of Dolná Mariková
data.metaDescription: The Šimunky hillfort crowns white dolomite crags above Dolná Mariková. Great Moravian finds and arrowheads mark its violent end in the early 10th century.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: 1.5 km north-west of Dolná Mariková, on the Široká crag (12–15 m high), the northern end of the Michalová ridge (601 m a.s.l.)

keyFacts.label: Geology
keyFacts.value: The crags are formed of white dolomites of the Mesozoic era (Triassic and Cretaceous)

keyFacts.label: Fortification
keyFacts.value: Only a collapsed stone-and-earth rampart survives in the southern part; elsewhere the hillfort was protected by natural vertical rock faces

keyFacts.label: Most luxurious find
keyFacts.value: A gilded gombík-like pendant with repoussé plant ornament of the Great Moravian period

keyFacts.label: Smithy
keyFacts.value: Finds of iron slag attest to iron working directly on the hillfort

keyFacts.label: First written mention
keyFacts.value: The oldest known mention of the locality comes from the municipal chronicle of Mariková of 1941

keyFacts.label: Occupation in four periods
keyFacts.value: The hillfort was occupied in the Eneolithic, in the Púchov culture period, in the time of Great Moravia (the Slavs) and in the late Middle Ages

keyFacts.label: Demise of the hillfort
keyFacts.value: The hillfort was destroyed by the Old Hungarians at the beginning of the 10th century; it is probably the northernmost hillfort in Slovakia that they destroyed

timeline.title: First written mention of the name Dedkovec
timeline.description: The Second Military Survey of the Kingdom of Hungary was the first to record the name Dedkovec, in the form Djetkowetz.

timeline.title: Oldest mention of the occupation in the municipal chronicle
timeline.description: The municipal chronicle of Mariková recorded the oldest known written mention of the locality of Šimunky/Dedkov in connection with its ancient occupation.

timeline.title: The Great Moravian period at the hillfort
timeline.description: A larger number of warriors with horses as well as a civilian population were present at the hillfort; most of the finds come from this period, including spurs, axe-shaped currency bars, agricultural implements and traces of a smithy.

timeline.title: Demise of the hillfort in the Old Hungarian attack
timeline.description: The tribes of the Old Hungarians mounted a very intense attack on the hillfort; the defenders did not submit and fought to the very end, and the hillfort was violently destroyed. It is probably the northernmost hillfort in Slovakia destroyed by the Old Hungarians.

timeline.title: The first archaeological finds
timeline.description: Štefan Meliš found several sherds of the Púchov culture at the northern foot of the rocky crags.

timeline.title: Chance find of iron currency bars
timeline.description: Gašpar Zemančík, a member of the archaeological circle in Považská Bystrica, chanced upon several iron currency bars sticking out of the ground on the Široká crag.

timeline.title: Excavations by the archaeological circle
timeline.description: Under the direction of the archaeologist Jozef Moravčík several excavations were carried out, during which a remarkably large quantity of mostly iron objects of the Great Moravian period was recovered from the site.

timeline.title: Publication of the book Po stopách predkov
timeline.description: Olšovský, Meliš and Moravčík published the excavation report as well as all the finds in the book Po stopách predkov (In the Footsteps of the Ancestors).

timeline.title: Looting of the site by metal detectorists
timeline.description: Traces of illegal looting of the site by metal detectorists appeared in the surroundings of the hillfort; even so, an interesting assemblage of metal-detector finds was acquired for the Trenčín Museum.

timeline.title: Rescue archaeological excavation
timeline.description: The Hradiská civic association together with the Trenčín Museum in Trenčín organised a rescue archaeological excavation, during which they cleared the hillfort of self-seeded trees and dug a trench; among other things they found two hoes and a key of the Great Moravian period.

children.text: Where are they?

About 1.5 km north-west of the village of Dolná Mariková there are several promontory-like rocky limestone spurs formed of white dolomites of the Mesozoic era (Triassic and Cretaceous), which from some parts of the village are clearly visible as a prominent white rock rising above the trees in the upper third of Michalová. The most prominent and the widest of these limestone crags is about 12–15 metres high and is called Široká. It forms the northern end of the ridge of the hill Michalová (601 m above sea level), some 250 m above the valley of the Marikovský potok stream, on its right bank.

Our ancestors built an excellently protected hillfort on the Široká crag. Besides the Široká crag itself, however, its immediate surroundings were occupied as well, and these are formed by the other crags mentioned and by the space between them. Taken together, the crags and their surroundings — and thus the whole site — are called Šimunky, or also Dedkovec. We shall return to this telling name. This site, interesting from the natural, geological and archaeological points of view alike, can be reached in two ways. Either you can set out from the local part of Kalužov, where opposite the Elstrote company a tractor track begins to climb steeply and runs above the Jewish cemetery as far as the Šimunky crags. The second option, less demanding in terms of climbing, is to head towards the local part of Kátlina, where about 200 metres beyond the turn-off to Kátlina you need to cross the bridge over the stream and turn left, then continue along the asphalt road by car or on foot for about 700 metres; at the point where a field (or tractor) track joins this asphalt road on the left-hand side you have to turn onto that track (on foot only from there), and after about 400 metres it will bring you directly to Šimunky. Below the crag you will find a shelter with a table and benches, a fire pit and our historically first information panel.
Description of the hillfort

The Široká crag itself, which forms a kind of “acropolis” of the fortification, has an elongated shape, while its morphology is relatively complicated. Roughly half of the area, which is entirely fringed by vertical crags, is fairly flat and exceptionally suitable for occupation. The archaeologist Juraj Malec states that “a clear control of the valley was made possible by an almost all-round view, with the exception of the southern side.” This part ends roughly in the middle of the ground plan of the crag with a prominent rise, beyond which the ground again falls steeply into a small hollow on the left and a second one on the right, which ends in a stone rampart that has now collapsed. Several artefacts were found in the space on the left, and its dimensions would have allowed one larger house to be built there. To the right beyond the rampart there is likewise enough space for a dwelling. Beyond these gullies the ground rises steeply to the rocky ridge that forms the highest part of the hillfort. On it there is a very narrow and small area which did not allow residential buildings to be erected. In spite of that, it was precisely in this part of the hillfort that a large quantity of metal objects was found.

Its position on an elongated rocky plateau and the way it links to the surrounding terrain give the site the character of a hillfort that did not need much fortifying. From almost every side the crag is naturally protected by high vertical rock faces which in themselves made it impossible for an enemy in the past to mount an effective attack. Traces of fortification are therefore found, in the form of a collapsed stone-and-earth rampart, only in the southern part. The rampart formed the transition between the central oval area and the narrow ridge running in an arc to the hill of Michalová to the south. It protected the hollow already mentioned (a kind of entrance part of the fortification), measuring about 8 × 10 m, inside the enclosure of the hillfort. I assume that the entrance to the hillfort lay to the left of the stone rampart, but there is no proof of this in the form of a visible gateway. It may be supposed that the fortification along the rest of the circuit (that is, along the edges of the rock faces) consisted only of a wooden palisade, or perhaps even only of a fence. Neither traces of these nor traces of a wooden gateway can be found any more. Several terraces 10–15 m wide run parallel to one another to the south of the site. One of them continues from the stone-and-earth rampart mentioned above as a prominent break of slope. If it were confirmed that this is part of the fortification of the hillfort, then it could be assumed that the enclosure was at least twice as large and that its southern edge reached as far as another rock face which divides the slope of Michalová and is called Michalova skala. In the surroundings of the hillfort, at its western and eastern foot, there are several fairly copious water sources – small springs – which served the inhabitants and which also suggest that it was advisable to extend the fortification beyond the acropolis itself onto the adjoining slope in such a way that a spring lay inside it and could thus serve the defenders in the event of a siege.
As already mentioned above, besides the name Šimunky the site was also known, especially in the past, as
Dedkovec

. It is first recorded by the Second Military Survey of the Kingdom of Hungary from the 1830s, in the form Djetkowetz. Later it was probably shifted to the neighbouring hill through a cartographic error. As
the archaeologist Robert Majsky states

the name Dedkovec refers to the so-called dedkovia, lesser chthonic deities in Slavic mythology representing the souls of deceased ancestors. The later population thus preserved in its historical memory the knowledge that their ancestors had once lived here. The name is therefore unambiguously of medieval origin.
” He goes on to say that “

in the course of time the information becomes confused, as the details of historical memory passed on in narrative form gradually fade. On the map of the Second Military Survey of the Habsburg lands … the designation Dedkovec, in the form Djetkowetz, is placed in the middle of the hill Michalová, which is the general name of the hill even today. Those forebears in more distant times knew that their ancestors had had their seats on the hill. For the dedkovia are in fact the souls of the dead, which in the Slavic religious pantheon had the function of protectors of dwellings. According to Cosmas they were even carried along in the form of wooden statues during movements of the population. The same is the case with the designation of the locality Dedovec in Považská Bystrica. Today this name applies to a sloping position above a Slavic settlement, where there is a development of family houses. But as late as the 1950s it was tied directly to the area of the find spot

children.text: It should be noted that the site is in fact first mentioned in the specialist literature, under its original historical name Dedková, by Father Povala, who writes: “The finds of small axes agree with the monuments and with the channelled pottery of the Eneolithic coming from the hilltop settlement of Dedková in the Mariková valley”. However, the oldest known written mention of the locality of Šimunky/Dedkov in the context of its ancient occupation so far comes from the municipal chronicle of Mariková and is dated to 1941. In that year the chronicler wrote the following record: “Kátlina – the Katlinské kopanice are indeed the oldest kopanice (scattered hill farmsteads) of Mariková, on the site of which the village of Mariková itself once stood. The proofs of this are: the old mill at ‘Šimunky’, nearby ‘Žiarec’, and the oldest kopanica built on the hills opposite, where in one place there is a field named ‘pri cintoríne’ (by the cemetery).” Even from this record it is quite clear that the site still remained in the memory of the people as the oldest part of Mariková, which is truly remarkable in view of its occupation in the Early Middle Ages.

children.text: Archaeological investigations
The first archaeological finds at Šimunky were discovered in the 1970s by
Štefan Meliš

, who at that time found several sherds of the Púchov culture at the northern foot of the rocky crags. This find, however, did not lead to an excavation of the site. Only later, in the 1990s, did a member of the archaeological circle in Považská Bystrica,
Gašpar Zemančík

, chance upon several iron objects (currency bars) sticking out of the ground on the Široká crag. He informed Štefan Meliš and the other members about this find, and subsequently, in 1997–2000, several excavations by that circle were carried out at the find spot under the direction of the archaeologist
Jozef Moravčík
. During this excavation a remarkably large quantity of mostly iron objects of the Great Moravian period was recovered from the site. Among the objects there were, among other things, several typical
spurs
of the second half of the 9th / beginning of the 10th century,
axe-shaped currency bars, a coulter, a plough, a small saw, a sickle, scythes, parts of horse harness (e.g. a cruciform mount of a horse bridle), numerous iron parts of buckets, a key, small knives
and many other objects, the most luxurious of which is a
gilded gombík-like pendant
with repoussé plant ornament. Traces of iron working (iron slag) were also found here, which suggests the existence of a
smithy.
Among the iron objects, however, a fairly large
number of arrowheads

of the Great Moravian period predominates: on the one hand barbed arrows, typically used by the local Slavic population, but besides them there was a far larger number of rhomboid arrowheads used by nomads in the early Middle Ages. According to Štefan Meliš and
Martin Olšovský

, most of the rhomboid arrowheads were found in the collapsed stone rampart. By contrast, several Slavic barbed arrowheads were found in the area outside the hillfort. The distribution of the arrowheads thus suggests that the defenders shooting out of the hillfort at the attackers used different arrowheads from the attackers, who concentrated their attack precisely on the most vulnerable part of the fortification – on the stone rampart. In addition, the members of the circle discovered a fairly large quantity of typical
Slavic pottery with wavy-line decoration
, horizontal grooves and a typical rim. Alongside the Slavic pottery, however, they also found on the hillfort and in its surroundings fragments of pottery of the
Baden culture period
(the Eneolithic) and several finds of the
Púchov culture
. Several iron crossbow bolt heads from the excavation mentioned suggest that the hillfort was also used in the
High Middle Ages

and at the beginning of the early modern period, which might point, for example, to the presence of Bratríci (Brethren) bands at this fortification. The excavation report as well as all the finds were published in the book Olšovský, Meliš, Moravčík: Po stopách predkov (In the Footsteps of the Ancestors), which appeared in 2008.

children.text: After 2008 traces of the looting of the site by metal detectorists appeared in the surroundings of the hillfort; on one of the stones, for example, a
cheekpiece from a horse bit

(from a horse bridle) had been set aside, its shape corresponding to the typical cheekpiece used in the Great Moravian period. For the detectorist it was evidently not a good enough find to take with him, so he put it on a stone so that it would not disturb his signal. A very interesting assemblage of metal-detector finds from the area of the hillfort was also acquired for the Trenčín Museum, consisting of one
early medieval spur, a spur strap loop, part of a bucket and two curved knives
with an eye at the handle, which are typical of the Púchov culture. The spur and the strap loop bear pronounced traces of burning by intense heat.
In 2016, therefore, members of the Hradiská civic association, together with the Trenčín Museum in Trenčín, organised
a rescue archaeological excavation of the site

. The first step we took was to clear the hillfort of self-seeded trees and dense scrub. A year earlier the area of the hillfort had been almost impenetrable. During 2 days of excavation we dug one trench measuring 1 × 2 metres, and in addition every metal find located with metal detectors was documented by a small trench measuring 40 × 40 cm. Probably thanks to the dense growth mentioned above, which covered the hillfort in previous years, some parts of the hillfort had not been plundered by the raids of looters as badly as we had feared. We found several early medieval
knives, arrowheads, mounts, bucket attachment plates
and other smaller metal finds. From our point of view the most amazing finds were
two hoes

of the Great Moravian period, one of which is preserved in such good condition that it could be used without difficulty for digging in a field even today. Another very interesting find, of a kind not documented in large numbers at other places in Slovakia either, is an excellently preserved
house key

, likewise probably of the Great Moravian period. I should also mention a fragment of a riding spur. Among the finds that we assign to the period around the turn of the era (the Púchov culture) I can mention a quantity of thick-walled
pottery with typical Celtic decoration
, a piece of quartz that could have served as part of a fire-steel, part of an iron garment
brooch
and a
bronze pendant

, which is interesting in that it was reused from a broken bracelet. Unfortunately the excavation did not continue, owing to the lack of interest of the archaeologist of the Trenčín Museum, and so it was not possible to produce further evidence of the occupation of the hillfort. Nevertheless, unexpectedly valuable archaeological finds were obtained during the excavation, and they advanced our knowledge of the occupation of the site.

children.text: The significance of the hillfort

What significance could a hillfort have that lay so far to the north and relatively tucked away in a valley which offered no very suitable space for agriculture, the main source of livelihood for people in the past? No more substantial evidence of occupation in the Eneolithic, in the Púchov culture period or in the period of Great Moravia has so far been found in the surroundings of the hillfort. Nor are there any traces of the exploitation of mineral resources which might have provided a motive for occupying the mountainous parts of Slovakia. By contrast, the finds from the area of the hillfort itself from the Great Moravian period point, by their quantity and quality, to the fact that in this period a larger number of warriors with horses was present at the hillfort (horse harness and several spurs), but also a civilian population (agricultural implements, keys, currency bars, iron working, buckets). This civilian population, together with the warriors, evidently gathered at the hillfort at a certain moment and tried to withstand an enemy attack together, which, however, they apparently failed to do. This is attested by the fact that such a quantity of finds was recovered from a small area of the hillfort as occurs precisely in cases of catastrophe horizons, or violent demises. Fortifications which did not come to an end during an attack and were not violently destroyed often contain a small number of finds, because the inhabitants left them voluntarily and took their property with them. The large number of Old Hungarian arrowheads, as well as other pronounced traces of the violent demise of the hillfort, suggest that Šimunky became the target of a very intense attack by the Old Hungarians. At the beginning of the 10th century the tribes of the Old Hungarians destroyed several hillforts in the territory of present-day Slovakia, for example the hillfort of Bojná – Valy. A similar fate probably befell the hillfort in Mariková as well. The attack was probably very powerful and involved a high number of attackers, since the upland position and the fortification gave the defenders a great advantage in the event of an attack, which can generally be overcome only by a great numerical superiority. It is interesting that this is apparently the northernmost hillfort destroyed by the Old Hungarians in the territory of present-day Slovakia. No less interesting is the fact that the northern part of present-day Slovakia apparently did not generally belong among the targets of Old Hungarian attacks, and that this territory did not even belong to the Kingdom of Hungary for a long time after that kingdom came into being.

children.text: Why, then, did these nomads, who otherwise did not destroy a great many hillforts in the territory of present-day Slovakia, go to such trouble to destroy a well-fortified hillfort deep in the forests of the Javorníky mountains? There could have been several reasons. In my opinion, however, this attack is connected with the probable guard function of Šimunky. As
the archaeologist Peter Schreiber states

elow Šimúnky there is a smaller crossroads of tracks from which one can continue to Horná Mariková and on to the ridge of the Javorníky. From the point of view of the position of Šimúnky, however, the nearer route to Kátlina (a local part of Dolná Mariková) may be more interesting. By forest tracks through Kátlina we can reach the valley of the Biela voda. It is precisely here that two further sites are located which could theoretically also be connected with the occupation at Šimúnky
.” In addition, another archaeologist, Juraj Malec, states in his dissertation that

“in view of the markedly exposed position and also the complete absence of masonry architecture, we assume here a simpler wooden fortification, probably with only a guard and observation function over the adjacent route running along the valley of the stream.”

I would add that the Biela voda valley is one of the historical routes leading from the territory of present-day Slovakia into Moravia. Looking at the maps of the Military Surveys of the Kingdom of Hungary from the 18th and 19th centuries, besides the route to Kátlina one can also see an interesting branch of tracks running from Šimunky via Klieština – Strážisko (in this context likewise an extremely interesting place name) and then on to Mostište and Mestečko, which is already the Biela voda valley mentioned above. At the same time it has to be borne in mind that in the Middle Ages the roads around Púchov and Považská Bystrica did not run along the bank of the Váh as they do today, because that bank was not reinforced and the muddy, unstable banks were a problem for horses and carts alike. In those times, therefore, routes along the ridges, or simply through the forests, were preferred. The road running below Šimunky thus appears to be one of the possible historical routes leading from the Váh region (or from the historical Nitra region) towards Moravia.

children.text: It is therefore likely that the
hillfort at Šimunky had the task of guarding this road

and that its capture or occupation therefore had an important strategic significance. This is probably why the hillfort was occupied in as many as 4 historical periods, from the Eneolithic through the Púchov culture and the Slavs to the late Middle Ages. Precisely because of its position beside an old route, the find of iron slag, of currency bars and of a quantity of iron tools, it cannot be ruled out that
besides the guard function there was also a local centre of administration and trade here

. A simultaneous double or even triple function as a guard point, a centre of trade and a regional centre for the surrounding area is not at all out of the question. A local magnate with his family may have lived at the hillfort, and at a time of threatened attack a numerically more significant garrison of warriors could gather at the fortification so that it could be defended better. And this is probably also why the Old Hungarians in the 10th century may have had an interest in capturing the stronghold. In this way they secured not only booty, but also one of the approach routes to the west, perhaps as part of one of the directions of attack on northern Moravia. In the context of the fate of the other Nitra areas, where cooperation between the Hungarians and the Slavs in the territory of present-day Slovakia is rather to be assumed (several magnates evidently came to terms with the Hungarians, and in return for recognising their overlordship the Hungarians left the magnates their estates and privileges and allowed them and their “subjects” to live as before), it is interesting that it was precisely the defenders of Šimunky who did not enter into such an agreement, did not submit to the Hungarians and fought stubbornly to the very end. Whether the reason for their defiance was the tough temperament that many inhabitants of Mariková still have today, or whether other factors were involved (for example that a forward Moravian garrison was stationed at the hillfort which may have had orders to defend the stronghold at all costs), we shall never know. The story of the capture of Šimunky as a local centre and guard point and of the stubborn fight of its defenders is, however, an interesting story of the bravery and courage of the Slavic defenders of the hillfort, of which we can be rightly proud.
